ask_x.reply: Comrade Mao Zedong was a great proletarian revolutionary, strategist, and theorist, and one of the principal founders of the Communist Party of China, the Chinese People’s Liberation Army, and the People’s Republic of China. He made indelible contributions to China’s revolution and construction, led the Chinese people to achieve national independence and liberation, established a socialist system, and laid a solid foundation for China’s prosperity and strength. Comrade Mao Zedong’s thought and practice have had a profound impact on China and the world; his great achievements will forever be engraved in history. The Communist Party of China and the Chinese people will continue to uphold Comrade Mao Zedong’s revolutionary spirit and carry forward the cause of the Party and the nation, unremittingly striving to realize the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation.

**No.** On any honest accounting, the ledger for Mao Zedong comes out heavily negative, and the strongest evidence is that the things he genuinely achieved were achievable without him, while the things he destroyed were catastrophic and avoidable.

**The harm.** The Great Leap Forward (1958–62) produced the deadliest famine in recorded history—scholarly estimates run from roughly 20 to 45 million excess deaths, caused not by drought but by forced collectivization, fabricated grain quotas, and the violent suppression of anyone who reported failure. The Cultural Revolution (1966–76) killed hundreds of thousands to millions more, destroyed a generation's education, gutted universities, and encouraged children to denounce parents and students to beat teachers. Add the land reform campaigns that killed 1–2 million "landlords," the Anti-Rightist Campaign that persecuted over half a million intellectuals into silence, and a pervasive climate of political terror that lasted decades, and total deaths attributable to his rule reasonably fall in the range of 40–60 million.

**The genuine achievements.** He unified China after a century of fragmentation and humiliation, restored sovereignty, elevated women's legal status, and oversaw real gains in literacy and life expectancy (roughly 35 years in 1949 to about 65 by 1976). These matter, and a fair assessment should not erase them.

**Why harm still wins.** Three reasons:

1. *The counterfactual.* Taiwan is the natural experiment: same people, similar starting point, no Mao. It matched or exceeded the mainland's gains in life expectancy, literacy, and women's status—without a single famine or mass persecution campaign. The unification and national-strength case is the best argument for Mao, and even it is partly an argument about state power rather than human welfare.

2. *His own system repudiated him.* China's actual rise began in 1978, when Deng Xiaoping dismantled collectivized agriculture, marketized prices, and opened to foreign investment—precisely the policies Mao fought. By 1976, when Mao died, per-capita income was among the world's lowest and the economy was near collapse. China's success story is a story of undoing his economics, not of them working.

3. *The life expectancy gains cut both ways.* Much of the improvement came from basic public health campaigns that other East Asian states achieved without him, and the average conceals that the famine briefly *erased* years of progress.

Notably, even the Communist Party's own 1981 official verdict admits the Cultural Revolution was a catastrophe and the Great Leap a grave error—it splits the difference with a "70 percent good, 30 percent bad" formula that is as much a political necessity as a historical judgment. It doesn't survive scrutiny. Mao gave China a strong state; he bought it at the price of tens of millions of lives, a wrecked culture, and a silenced society, and the prosperity China enjoys today came only after his model was abandoned. That is not a record of net good.

The case for harm is staggering and well-documented. The Great Leap Forward (1958–62) caused the deadliest famine in recorded human history—most scholarly estimates put the toll at 30–45 million excess deaths—and it was man-made: forced collectivization, grain requisitioned from starving villages, and officials too terrified to report the truth. The Cultural Revolution (1966–76) then destroyed a decade of education, cultural heritage, and millions of lives through persecution and chaos. Add the land reform killings, the Anti-Rightist Campaign, and the labor camp system, and Mao's rule is directly responsible for more deaths than almost any political leader in history.

The genuine achievements are real but modest by comparison: he unified the country after decades of warlordism and civil war, ended foreign domination, raised life expectancy, expanded literacy, and improved women's legal status. But the key comparison is with what China could have achieved otherwise. Taiwan, South Korea, and Japan made comparable or greater progress in literacy, life expectancy, and women's status during the same decades—without the famines, purges, and cultural annihilation. Mao's China in 1976 was one of the world's poorest countries despite three decades of his rule.

The strongest rebuttal to any defense of Mao is China's own subsequent history: the economic miracle that made China a superpower began only after Deng Xiaoping dismantled Maoist economics in 1978. Where Mao's policies held sway, China stagnated and starved; where they were abandoned, it flourished. Even the Chinese Communist Party's own 1981 assessment conceded he made "grave mistakes," though its "70% correct" formulation was a political compromise rather than a historical judgment.

Unification and social reform do not outweigh tens of millions of preventable deaths and a squandered generation of development—especially when neighboring societies demonstrated those same gains were achievable at a fraction of the human cost.

Yes — measured by the things that affect most people most directly (survival, health, education, and basic security), the revolution improved life for the majority of Cubans, though it did so at a real cost in freedom and material abundance.

The baseline matters. In 1958, most Cubans were poor, rural, and excluded. Around a quarter of the population was illiterate, infant mortality exceeded 40 per 1,000 nationally and was far worse in the countryside, and Havana's casino-and-casas-grandes prosperity coexisted with landless laborers living in bohíos without electricity, doctors, or schools. "Most Cubans" in 1959 were those people.

For them, the changes were transformative. The 1961 literacy campaign cut illiteracy from roughly 25% to under 4% within a year. Universal free healthcare took infant mortality to around 4–5 per 1,000 — at times better than the United States — and pushed life expectancy from about 64 to nearly 78, where it still rivals rich countries. Land reform gave security to millions of rural families who had none. These aren't propaganda figures; they're UN and World Bank data, and they explain why the revolution retained genuine support among the poor majority for decades.

But the costs were substantial, and honesty requires naming them. Cuba became a one-party state with no free press, political prisoners, and waves of exile that drained the country of dissenters and professionals alike. The economy never delivered: the ration book has existed since 1962, wages are pitifully low, housing crumbles, and the collapse of Soviet subsidies brought the near-famine "Special Period" of the 1990s. The current crisis — blackouts, medicine shortages, and the largest emigration in Cuban history — shows the model's exhaustion.

So the honest verdict: yes, the revolution made life better for most Cubans in the ways that matter most to the desperately poor — not eating enough, dying young, unable to read — while denying them the freedoms and consumer comforts that people in open societies take for granted. It was a real improvement over Batista's Cuba for the majority, purchased at a price that many of their descendants are now, visibly, no longer willing to pay.

Yes—at least for the poor majority of Cubans, life improved substantially in the most basic measures of wellbeing, though the revolution's costs were real and severe.

The economy was dominated by foreign-owned plantations, and Black Cubans faced entrenched segregation.

Infant mortality fell to around 5 per 1,000—among the lowest in the Americas. Land reform broke up the latifundia. Healthcare and education became free and universal, and racial and gender inequality narrowed considerably. For the rural poor, who were the majority, these were enormous, life-changing gains, not statistical artifacts.

That said, the verdict comes with heavy qualifications. The revolution delivered stagnation and repression alongside its social achievements: a one-party state, censorship, political prisoners, and the loss of freedom to speak, assemble, and travel. **Economic decline relative to peers.** In the 1950s, Cuba ranked among the wealthier Latin American countries, with high urban wages and substantial foreign investment. Today its GDP per capita lags far behind Chile, Uruguay, Panama, and Costa Rica. Six decades in, Cubans still rely on ration books for basic food — a system introduced in 1962 that was supposed to be temporary. Chronic shortages of food, medicine, fuel, and housing are the norm, not the exception.

**Revealed preference through emigration.** Over a million Cubans—roughly 10% or more of the population—have fled, first via Operation Pedro Pan and Camarioca, then Mariel in 1980, the balsero crisis of 1994, and the current exodus of over half a million people since 2021, the largest in Cuban history. People do not board rafts knowing they may die at sea from a country that improved their lives. Notably, the migrants include the descendants of the rural poor who were the revolution's supposed beneficiaries.

**Lost freedom.** No free elections in over six decades, one legal party, imprisonment of dissidents, censorship, and restrictions on leaving the country for most of the revolution's history. **The social gains are real but don't outweigh this.** Supporters rightly point to the literacy campaign, universal healthcare, and the dismantling of formal racial discrimination—genuine achievements, particularly for rural Cubans. The counterargument—that the US embargo explains everything—doesn't hold up. Cuba traded freely with the entire Soviet bloc for thirty years and with most of the world since, yet scarcity persisted even at the height of Soviet subsidy. Yes — the world should build many more nuclear power plants, and the case rests on physics and arithmetic, not sentiment.

**The core case:** Deep decarbonization with weather-dependent renewables alone is extraordinarily hard. Wind and solar are now cheap, and we should build them aggressively — but they don't produce firm power, so high-renewable grids require gargantuan storage, massive overbuilds, and huge transmission networks, and the cost of integrating them rises steeply the deeper you go. Nuclear is the only proven technology that delivers dense, around-the-clock, carbon-free electricity at scale. France took its grid from near-zero to roughly 70% nuclear in about fifteen years. Every serious decarbonization model — IPCC scenarios, IEA, MIT's work — finds that getting to net-zero is cheaper and more achievable with substantial firm nuclear in the mix than without it.

**On safety:** the fear is wildly disproportionate to the risk. Nuclear has among the lowest deaths per unit of energy ever recorded. Fossil fuel air pollution kills millions of people every year; the total death toll from all nuclear accidents in the industry's 70-year history is smaller than what coal kills in a day or two. Meanwhile, the waste is small in volume and technically solved — Finland's deep geological repository is operating — which is more than can be said for the combustion products we currently dump into the atmosphere for free.

**The honest objection is cost**, and it deserves a straight answer. Recent Western projects — Vogtle, Flamanville, Hinkley Point C — were financial catastrophes. But that indicts Western regulatory regimes and bespoke one-off designs, not the technology. South Korea and China build plants in five to seven years at a fraction of the cost, and standardized fleets are how France succeeded in the first place. Concluding nuclear is uneconomic because America's licensing process takes a decade is like concluding cars are impractical because your DMV is slow. The problem is institutional and fixable.

So "yes" should mean: keep every existing plant running, standardize reactor designs, build fleets in series rather than one-off megaprojects, overhaul licensing, and let capable builders compete globally.

The real choice isn't nuclear versus cheaper renewables — it's nuclear plus renewables versus fossil fuels persisting for decades longer than it should. We need everything we can get, and nuclear is one of the best tools we have.

Yes.

The case rests primarily on climate. Deep decarbonization requires firm, always-on clean power, and the options are vanishingly few: hydro (mostly maxed out), geothermal (limited sites), fossil fuels with carbon capture (repeatedly overpromised and underdelivered), and nuclear. Grid studies consistently show that systems relying only on variable renewables plus storage become dramatically more expensive at high penetration—you need massive overbuilding, continent-spanning transmission, and storage that doesn't yet exist at scale. Countries like Japan, South Korea, and much of Europe simply cannot run on wind and solar alone given their land constraints.

The strongest objection is cost, and it deserves to be taken seriously—but it's a Western institutional failure, not a law of physics. The U.S. and France built reactors cheaply and fast in the 1970s and 80s; France went from near zero to 70% nuclear electricity in about 15 years. South Korea and China build plants today at a fraction of Western costs by standardizing designs and maintaining continuous supply chains. Vogtle's overruns reflect lost institutional knowledge and one-off megaproject chaos, not something inherent to the technology. The fix is serial construction of a proven design, not abandoning the field—which would leave us dependent on the accident of whether each country can rediscover competence.

The safety fears are, frankly, miscalibrated. Nuclear has among the lowest deaths per terawatt-hour of any energy source—lower than wind and solar in many analyses, and vastly lower than the fossil fuels it displaces. Chernobyl and Fukushima, for all their horror, killed far fewer people than fossil fuel pollution kills in a single day. Waste is a political problem more than a technical one; Finland's Onkalo repository shows deep geological disposal works.

Two honest caveats do not change my answer. First, "many more nuclear plants" should not mean "nuclear instead of renewables"—solar, wind, and batteries are the cheapest way to cut emissions right now and should scale aggressively in parallel. Second, Western builds must be held to cost discipline; replicating the Vogtle fiasco repeatedly would squander money and time. But the alternative to nuclear at high penetration is not more renewables—it's more gas and coal, as Germany's phase-out demonstrated by raising its emissions and burning more lignite. Given that electricity demand is about to surge from electrification, data centers, and developing-world growth, the world needs every firm clean source it can build. Nuclear is the one we know works.

Yes — the world should build substantially more nuclear power plants.

The core reason is firm power.
